content: 1. A patient with Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) who exhibits an unexpectedly severe clinical course, even if another pathogen was initially identified, and does not respond to appropriate treatment, should be further evaluated. 2. A patient with SARI who has had recent exposure to animals should be considered for additional investigation. 3. An immunocompromised patient presenting with an acute illness that cannot be fully explained by another pathogen warrants further diagnostic evaluation. 4. Close contacts of confirmed or probable MERS-CoV cases should be identified and monitored for respiratory symptoms for 14 days following their last exposure to the symptomatic case. 5. Any contact who develops symptoms during this period should be tested for MERS-CoV. 6. If feasible, all contacts, especially healthcare workers and other inpatient hospital contacts, should be identified and tested for MERS-CoV, regardless of symptom development. 7. A detailed record of all contacts and co-exposed individuals should be maintained, including demographic information, dates of first and last common exposure or contact with the case, and the onset date of fever or respiratory symptoms if they develop. 8. For any contacts who become infected with MERS-CoV, common exposures and the type of contact with the confirmed or probable case should be thoroughly documented. 9. Close contacts should be monitored daily (e.g., through visits or telephone calls) for the development of fever, acute respiratory illness, or other symptoms for 14 days after their last exposure to the initial case. 10. Contacts should be advised to contact healthcare workers immediately if they develop symptoms. 11. If any contacts are confirmed to have MERS-CoV infection, their close contacts should also be monitored. 12. Symptomatic contacts under investigation should limit their interactions with healthy individuals and practice good respiratory hygiene to prevent onward transmission. 13. Current guidance on preventing transmission in households and healthcare facilities is available on the WHO MERS website. 14. Decisions regarding the admission of symptomatic cases or contacts should be based on clinical judgment and concerns about further transmission. 15. If symptomatic individuals are managed at home, they should be closely monitored for progression of their illness. 16. It is currently not possible to predict the course of illness for an individual patient. 17. In addition to monitoring close contacts for acute illness and testing with PCR, it is strongly advised to collect sera from all close contacts, including healthcare workers. 18. This will help identify mild and asymptomatic MERS-CoV infections and define common exposures in the environment or to the case that might result in infection. 19. Investigators should collect acute sera from all close contacts immediately after the confirmed or probable case is identified. 20. Sera collection should be repeated in close contacts 3–4 weeks later, regardless of whether contacts have developed symptoms. 21. If the index case was ill more than 3–4 weeks before the investigation, only a single serum specimen needs to be collected from contacts. 22. For each contact, information should be collected regarding any illness during the intervening period, including all signs and symptoms and their severity. 23. Specific exposures to the confirmed or suspected case, such as providing care, exposure to body fluids, physical contact, duration and proximity of exposure, eating with, or sleeping in the same room as the case, should be documented. 24. Exposures to camels, unprocessed food and beverages, and other social and environmental contacts should also be recorded. 25. Efforts to identify additional cases beyond close contacts are critical for infection prevention and control and to determine the total extent of transmission in the community. 26. Active case finding in the area under investigation should focus on patients currently admitted to healthcare facilities in the community where the confirmed MERS-CoV case was discovered. 27. Any patients currently in the hospital with unexplained SARI should be considered for MERS-CoV testing. 28. Patients meeting the case definition should be tested for MERS-CoV. 29. Patients who recently died of an unexplained illness consistent with the case definition should be tested for MERS-CoV infection if appropriate clinical specimens are available. 30. Surveillance in the area under investigation should be enhanced to detect cases that might arise subsequent to the discovery of the index case. 31. The geographical area targeted will need to be assessed on a case-by-case basis and defined by the suspected exposures of the case under investigation. 32. Enhanced surveillance should last for a minimum of one month, depending on the findings of the investigation and whether there is evidence of sustained transmission in the area. 33. Enhancements include daily reporting, data management, and dissemination to relevant stakeholders. 34. Laboratory molecular testing capacity for MERS-CoV should be introduced in local healthcare facilities, or mechanisms for rapid specimen transfer to capable laboratories should be established. 35. If SARI surveillance is in place, it should be expanded to other facilities in the area. If not, SARI surveillance should be initiated at healthcare facilities in the community of the case. 36. Testing for MERS-CoV in SARI cases at local healthcare facilities in the area under investigation should be increased. 37. If resources allow, consider testing milder cases of influenza-like illness presenting to surveillance sites. 38. To confirm the presence of MERS-CoV in suspect cases, appropriate clinical specimens should be collected for testing. 39. Lower respiratory tract specimens, such as sputum, endotracheal aspirates, or bronchial alveolar lavage, are preferred as they contain higher virus titres and are more sensitive for detecting the virus. 40. Upper respiratory tract specimens, such as nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs, should be collected if lower respiratory tract specimens cannot be obtained. 41. If initial testing of an upper respiratory specimen is negative in a patient suspected of having MERS-CoV infection, repeat testing should be performed. 42. Blood should be collected for serological testing. For recent cases, an initial blood specimen should be collected, and a repeat specimen taken after at least 3 weeks. 43. MERS-CoV has been identified in other body fluids, including blood, urine, and stool of infected patients, but virus titres in these fluids are low and may not be useful for diagnostic testing. 44. Healthcare workers collecting clinical specimens should use appropriate infection control measures, including personal protective equipment. 45. PCR is the most widely used method for detecting the presence of the virus. At least three sites in the virus genome (e.g., upE, ORF1a, ORF1b) have been identified as suitable targets for such assays. 46. Positive controls for the upE screening and ORF1a confirmation assays are available. A confirmed case should have positive test results for at least two different sites in the virus genome or a positive result for a single site plus sequencing of a different site showing close similarity to known virus sequences. 47. Testing should be carried out in laboratories experienced in performing these procedures, and specimens should be sent to a reference laboratory for confirmation. 48. A Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) facility, including the use of a microbiological safety cabinet, is required for handling specimens thought to contain MERS-CoV when performing RNA extraction for PCR. 49. Recommendations on laboratory biorisk management for MERS-CoV have been prepared. 50. Serological testing is essential for identifying mild and asymptomatic infections and validating assays under development. 51. Viral culture of MERS-CoV should only be attempted in specialized laboratories with appropriate biosafety level 3 capabilities. 52. Specimens testing positive for MERS-CoV should be genetically sequenced, and the data uploaded to publicly accessible databases. 53. Both partial and whole genome sequencing provide crucial information about the origin and source of exposure to MERS-CoV. 54. Infection control measures, including the use of personal protective equipment and isolation of confirmed and probable cases, are critical to reducing nosocomial transmission. 55. Symptomatic contacts or probable cases with mild symptoms should be considered for close observation in a medical facility due to the risk of rapid progression to severe complications. 56. Data analysis should include descriptive analysis of cases in terms of person, place, and time, as well as estimation of incubation periods, transmission patterns, and disease severity. 57. Case-control studies should investigate specific exposures and risk factors for infection by comparing cases to community controls. 58. Studies of healthcare exposures should examine the occurrence of infection in persons exposed to confirmed cases in healthcare settings, using molecular diagnostics and serological testing.
